notes.meaning: Samuel pours oil over Saul's head to set him apart as king, kisses him as a sign of respect and friendship, and announces God's choice. Calling Israel the Lord's inheritance reminded Saul that the people belonged to God, and the king was only a servant caring for them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teachers such as Augustine saw the anointing of Israel's kings as a sacred foreshadowing of Jesus, who is the true Christ and Anointed One.

notes.meaning: Samuel gives Saul a exact sign to prove that God really spoke through him. Meeting men who report that the lost donkeys were found would lift Saul's family worries and show that God knows every detail of daily life.

Saul is told he will meet three worshipers carrying sacrificial gifts near Bethel, and they will hand him two loaves of bread. This second sign provided Saul with food and served as a quiet preview of people bringing honor and tribute to their future king.

At Gibeah, where Philistine troops had a military post, Saul would encounter a band of prophets coming down from worship with musical instruments. These prophets served the Lord by singing praises and teaching God's truth accompanied by music.

Samuel promises that God's Spirit will suddenly come with power upon Saul, enabling him to praise God openly alongside the prophets. This divine touch would change him from an ordinary farm worker into a bold and capable leader ready to govern.

Once these three signs come true, Saul is instructed to act boldly whenever opportunities arise to lead and protect the people. He could move forward with courage because God had promised to be with him.

Samuel directs Saul to go to Gilgal and wait a full seven days until the prophet arrives to offer sacrifices and provide God's instructions. This command tested Saul's patience and reminded him that the king must always remain obedient to God's word through His prophet.

The moment Saul walked away from Samuel, God changed his heart, and every promised sign came true before the day ended. God replaced Saul's hesitation with the wisdom and courage needed to lead a nation.

differ.view: This change was not inward spiritual regeneration or salvation, but special civic gifts and bravery suited for governing.
God gave Saul a genuine measure of holiness and spiritual power for leadership, which he later forfeited through disobedience.

notes.meaning: When Saul reached Gibeah, the band of prophets met him just as Samuel had said. The Spirit of God came upon Saul with great power, and he joined them in their inspired songs of praise.

Neighbors and acquaintances who knew Saul's past were astonished to see him singing and praising God with the prophets. Because Saul had never been religious or trained in such circles, his sudden change became a topic of public wonder.

A bystander answered the crowd's surprise by asking who the father of the prophets was, pointing out that God gives prophetic gifts freely rather than through family heritage. This event gave rise to a popular proverb used whenever someone did something completely unexpected.
After the inspiration ceased, Saul went up to the local place of worship. He went there to thank the Lord for what had happened and to seek guidance for the future.

Saul's uncle questioned Saul and his servant about where they had been during their long absence. Saul explained simply that after searching everywhere for the lost donkeys, they went to seek Samuel's help.

Curious about a private visit with the renowned prophet, Saul's uncle pressed him to share everything Samuel had said. The uncle likely sensed that something unusual had taken place during the meeting.

Saul told his uncle that Samuel confirmed the donkeys were safe, but kept completely quiet about being chosen as king. His silence reflected modesty and careful patience, trusting God to reveal the kingship at the right time.

Samuel called all the leaders and people together before the Lord at Mizpah for a formal national assembly. This was the place where Israel had previously repented and seen God win a great victory over the Philistines.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the public assembly at Mizpah as coming from a separate tradition that was later combined with the story of Saul's private anointing.

notes.meaning: Speaking for the Lord, Samuel reminded the Israelites that God had delivered them out of slavery in Egypt and rescued them from every foreign oppressor. God had never failed to defend His people whenever they trusted Him.

Samuel confronted the nation with their sin of demanding an earthly king, which amounted to rejecting God as their true protector. He then directed the tribes and family clans to step forward so God could publicly identify their new ruler.

Samuel cast sacred lots before the Lord, narrowing the choice from all Israel down to the tribe of Benjamin, then to the clan of Matri, and finally to Saul himself. When Saul was announced as the chosen king, the crowd searched for him, but he was nowhere to be seen.

The people asked the Lord whether the chosen man had even arrived at the gathering, and the Lord revealed that Saul was hiding among the baggage carts. Saul hid himself out of genuine modesty and fear of such a heavy calling.
The people ran and brought Saul out of hiding to stand before the entire assembly. His tall stature made him stand out visibly, rising a head above everyone else in the crowd.

Samuel presented Saul as the man chosen by the Lord, noting that there was no one quite like him among all the people. The assembly accepted him with enthusiasm, shouting out the royal salute wishing long life to their king.

Samuel carefully explained the rules and rights that governed the kingship, wrote them down on a scroll, and placed it before the Lord for safekeeping. These laws limited the king's power and reminded both king and people to obey God's covenant.

Saul returned quietly to his home in Gibeah, accompanied by a group of valiant men whose hearts God had touched to support him. God gave these loyal men the desire to protect and honor their newly appointed leader.

Some rebellious and troublemaking men openly sneered at Saul, questioning his ability to save Israel and refusing to bring him customary gifts of respect. Saul demonstrated self-control and wisdom by choosing to hold his peace rather than retaliate.
